315.bp: When you ask a system for a movie recommendation, most just spit back a number. But what if the system could ask you clarifying questions, reason through your needs, invoke tools to look things up, and chat with you until it really gets it right? That's what an interactive recommendation agent does—it turns a passive lookup into an active conversation. The goal is to train these agents to actually get better at having these conversations by learning from what works.
315.wh: The obstacle is that training these agents with reinforcement learning is messy on three fronts. First, when an agent makes ten decisions in a row to help you, it's hard to figure out which specific decisions actually led to a good outcome (credit assignment). Second, if the agent can choose from thousands of possible actions at each step, exploring enough to find good ones becomes slow and wasteful. Third, the agent needs to learn multiple different skills—asking questions, looking things up, continuing dialogue—all at once without them interfering with each other.
315.ap: The paper proposes GIMO, which borrows an idea from human motivation: instead of waiting for a final reward signal, treat the learning process itself as fulfilling three intrinsic drives—Autonomy (agent has choices), Competence (agent gets better), and Relatedness (agent helps the user). At each step, the system estimates an intrinsic reward based on these drives by asking a generative model to predict what future states look like. These intrinsic rewards kick in immediately and locally, so credit assignment is easier. The system also uses these predictions to suggest good actions to explore, so the agent explores smarter rather than randomly.
315.ww: This works because intrinsic rewards give the agent immediate feedback on whether each decision moved toward a good outcome, without needing to wait for the conversation to end. Predicting future states lets the system see which actions expand possibilities (autonomy), improve skill (competence), or better serve the user (relatedness). These three drivers align with what actually makes recommendation conversations work in the real world—the agent feels empowered, learns efficiently, and stays focused on helping the user.
315.po: The result is that training becomes faster and more stable, the agent explores better without random flailing, and multiple skills (questioning, tool use, dialogue) improve together without sabotaging each other. The abstract shows this solves a practical bottleneck: you can now train interactive agents without needing expensive human annotations of every good conversation.

316.bp: Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) are the bouncers at the door of a website—they read incoming requests and block anything that looks like an attack (like code injection). The question is: can you slip a real attack past the bouncer by disguising its structure in a way the bouncer and the server interpret differently?
316.wh: The problem is that HTTP/2, the protocol websites use to talk to clients, lets messages be organized in different structural ways (priorities and dependencies between message streams) that should be equivalent from a logic standpoint. A WAF might read one structure and miss an attack, but the backend server might reorganize that same message into another structure and execute the attack. If the WAF and server disagree on how to interpret the structure, an attacker can slip through.
316.ap: The researchers craft what are called Stream Parser Confusion Attacks (SPCA): they take a normal, harmless-looking message structure and rearrange the priority trees and dependencies (which streams depend on which other streams) according to three patterns: skewed trees, k-ary trees, and unbalanced trees. The actual malicious content stays identical and unchanged—only the wrapping structure changes. They test this against 13 WAFs and 20 real web frameworks to see if the WAF blocks it while the server accepts it.
316.ww: This works because HTTP/2 allows multiple valid ways to express the same logical dependencies, but WAFs and servers may each have their own parser that makes different choices about how to flatten or interpret those trees. If the WAF parses strictly and the server is lenient (or vice versa), they see different payloads. The protocol itself permits the ambiguity; attackers just exploit that freedom.
316.po: Across three tree patterns, bypass rates ranged from 44% to 50% on real WAFs—meaning nearly half of deployed firewalls can be evaded by simply reorganizing the structure of an HTTP/2 stream, with no modification to the actual attack. This reveals a concrete gap in how WAFs and servers handle protocol ambiguity, and it matters because HTTP/2 is widely deployed.

317.bp: In wireless networks, devices need to sense whether a radio frequency band is in use (occupied by someone else's signal) before they transmit. The real-world constraint: a single device has limited battery, antenna time, and hardware, so it can only listen to a few frequencies at a time. How do you figure out what's happening in the entire radio spectrum when you can only see pieces of it?
317.wh: The traditional approach assumes you can monitor one band at a time or have perfect data for every frequency. But in practice, you get fragmented, incomplete snapshots. New frequency bands appear with no historical data to learn from. Different parts of the spectrum are correlated (if one frequency is occupied, nearby ones might be too), but you can't see those correlations if you only observe a few bands. This creates a training bottleneck: the machine learning model doesn't have enough complete examples to learn properly.
317.ap: The paper treats the entire radio spectrum as a graph, where each frequency band is a node and edges connect related bands. Each device only observes its own small subgraph of frequencies. Then they use a hyperbolic graph neural network (a type of neural net designed to handle hierarchical structures) to learn features from both the full graph and the individual subgraphs. The key is that devices share what they learn collaboratively, so everyone benefits from everyone else's partial observations without sharing raw sensor data.
317.ww: This works because real-world spectrum has structure: frequencies at similar ranges have similar behavior, and events in one band suggest things about neighbors. By modeling that structure as a graph and using a neural net that respects hierarchical relationships, the system can infer the overall pattern even from scattered, incomplete observations. Collaboration lets each device learn from the pattern detected by others.
317.po: The system can now detect occupied spectrum bands across many frequencies simultaneously, even when each device can only physically sense a small slice. This matters because it lets wireless networks coexist (e.g., mobile networks and Wi-Fi) without constantly interfering with each other—devices can sense the whole picture from partial views.

318.bp: Open-source code repositories like NPM (for JavaScript) and PyPI (for Python) are under attack by criminals who sneak malicious code into packages. The code looks normal but steals credentials, mines cryptocurrency, or triggers later when an unsuspecting developer uses it. How do you spot these poisoned packages before thousands of developers download them?
318.wh: Detection is hard because attackers don't use obvious signatures anymore. Simple rule-based filters (e.g., 'if the code contains keyword X, block it') are easy to evade with slight variations. Machine learning models trained on past attacks might miss novel disguises. And when you see a new package, you often have no context—just the code itself, with no history or comparison cases to judge against.
318.ap: IntelGuard takes a different path: it builds a knowledge base from 8,000+ real threat reports written by security experts, capturing not just malicious code snippets but also descriptions of *what those snippets do* and *why experts flagged them*. When a new package arrives, the system retrieves the most similar examples from this knowledge base using semantic search (finding reports about code that does similar things), then uses a large language model guided by expert reasoning to decide if the new package's behavior matches the known attack patterns.
318.ww: This works because expert knowledge captures the *intent* and *mechanism* of attacks, not just the syntactic code. A stolen variable name or obfuscation might fool a simple filter, but it can't fool reasoning grounded in expert understanding of what the code actually *does*. Retrieving similar past cases gives the system concrete comparisons to ground its reasoning in.
318.po: On a real test of 4,027 packages, the system achieved 99% accuracy and caught 54 previously unknown malicious packages when deployed on PyPI. It also maintained 96.5% accuracy even on obfuscated (intentionally scrambled) code. This matters because it shifts detection from fragile rules to interpretable reasoning based on expert knowledge.

319.bp: Imagine recommendation systems at different companies (one for music, one for movies) that want to pool their learning but can't share customer data due to privacy laws. Each company trains its own local model, they coordinate without touching raw data, and they all get better together. Now complicate it: they want to use large language models, which don't learn explicit user profiles but instead encode knowledge through predicting text. How do you coordinate learning across LLM-based recommenders?
319.wh: LLM-based recommenders are slippery: they don't learn clear, comparable user embeddings the way old systems did. When each company updates its local LLM based on its own users, the magnitude and direction of those updates vary wildly across companies because their user bases are different. When aggregating updates from different domains, you end up with either noise that washes out the learning or updates that are biased heavily toward the largest domain. And measuring similarity between what different LLMs learn is hard because their internal representations are implicit.
319.ap: FeDecider tackles this by forcing each company's local updates to have a consistent structure: it decomposes each update into a low-rank component (the essential change) and filters out noise. Then it shares only the *direction* of each update (which way is better) but not the *magnitude* (how strong the change was). This normalizes across domains so a small company's insight isn't drowned out. For handling LLMs' implicit knowledge, it uses additional regularization to keep the shared learning coordinated without revealing internal representations.
319.ww: This works because direction-only aggregation is scale-invariant: a company training 1,000 users and a company training 1 million users both contribute equally in terms of learned direction. The low-rank factorization lets noise cancel out without losing the real signal. By regularizing the aggregation, you ensure that each local LLM-based recommender is being steered toward similar objectives without needing to see or compare their internal knowledge.
319.po: The result is that LLM-based recommenders can now learn collaboratively across privacy boundaries without each company dominating the aggregate, and without revealing proprietary user data or model internals. This enables privacy-preserving cross-domain recommendation at scale.

320.bp: Graphs are everywhere—social networks, recommendation systems, knowledge bases. When building a machine learning model on graph data, you normally need labeled examples (e.g., 'this user likes this category'). But labeling is expensive. How do you learn useful patterns from an unlabeled graph on your own, without human annotations?
320.wh: Most graph learning methods ignore high-frequency signals—local structure, fine-grained connections between nearby nodes. These signals are valuable for capturing detailed patterns but are easy to overfit on: if the model learns too heavily on local details specific to one dataset, it fails on new graphs. The tension is that you need local structure for accuracy but avoiding memorization requires using global patterns too.
320.ap: FC-GSSL (Frequency-Corrupt Based Graph Self-Supervised Learning) deliberately corrupts the graph by removing nodes and edges in ways that preserve low-frequency information but destroy high-frequency details. These corrupted versions are fed into an autoencoder (a model that compresses and reconstructs data). The autoencoder is trained to reconstruct the *low-frequency* parts, forcing it to learn high-frequency details indirectly by figuring out what was missing. To avoid overfitting to any single corruption pattern, the method generates multiple corrupted versions using different sampling strategies and trains on their union and intersection.
320.ww: This works because learning what was removed is an indirect way of learning what matters locally. By forcing the model to explain the low-frequency signal while the high-frequency details are hidden, you force it to infer those details rather than memorize them. Using multiple corruption patterns prevents the model from exploiting any single corruption bias, so it learns robust, generalizable high-frequency patterns.
320.po: The model learns rich representations from unlabeled graphs by fusing high- and low-frequency information, without needing labels. This matters because it reduces the labeling burden for tasks like recommendation (predicting which users like items) and social network analysis (predicting community structure).

321.bp: In online advertising, a company advertises across multiple platforms—Google, Facebook, Instagram—simultaneously. Each platform has its own audience, costs, and user behavior. The challenge is deciding how much budget to spend on each platform, how to bid for users on each, and how to adjust those decisions as market conditions change. The goal is to maximize return on investment (ROI) across all channels.
321.wh: Optimization-based methods can compute the mathematically best allocation if the world were static, but advertising markets change constantly (competitor bids go up, user behavior shifts). Reinforcement learning (RL) can adapt to changes, but RL is built around a simple state-action-reward loop that struggles to encode the *sequence* of decisions and constraints (e.g., 'don't spend more than $5,000 on Facebook this week'). RL often gets stuck ignoring important historical patterns or violating constraints it wasn't penalized hard enough for breaking.
321.ap: AHBid combines two ingredients: a high-level planner using a diffusion model (a generative model that gradually refines a rough idea into a detailed plan) to propose budget allocations and constraint strategies, and a real-time controller that fine-tunes bids moment-to-moment. The diffusion planner ingests historical spending patterns and predicts good budget distributions. Then a constraint-enforcement layer ensures spending rules are honored. Finally, a trajectory refinement layer re-uses historical data to adapt the plan when the market shifts unexpectedly.
321.ww: This works because diffusion models are good at capturing complex, high-dimensional distributions (like 'what does a good multi-channel spend look like?') from training examples, so the planner naturally respects patterns in historical data. Real-time control then adjusts within that plan. Splitting planning (long-term, data-rich) from control (short-term, reactive) lets each piece do what it's good at, while constraint enforcement stays explicit and auditable.
321.po: The system balances adaptation to market changes with respect for spending constraints and historical patterns. It matters because it lets advertisers deploy capital across channels efficiently without constantly re-optimizing from scratch or violating their budget rules.

322.bp: When governments, cities, or organizations make big decisions—about climate policy, healthcare spending, infrastructure—they rely on data and analysis to inform negotiations. But data isn't neutral: how it's collected, which questions you ask, and which models you use can predetermine outcomes before the human deliberation even begins. The big picture question is: how does big data and AI reshape bargaining power and the substance of negotiations?
322.wh: This is not a technical engineering paper but a literature review asking a social question. The tension is that data appears objective—just numbers and facts—so decision-makers often treat it as destiny ('the data says we must do X'). But whoever controls the data collection and framing actually has power over what gets negotiated and what's deemed 'feasible.' This is hard to see because the power operates invisibly through definitions and metrics.
322.ap: The authors surveyed over 1,000 citations across sociology, environmental science, health policy, media studies, and computer science, extracting four themes: how big data structures the space of possible negotiation outcomes, how algorithms shape which topics get public attention, how AI tools influence decision-making and final agreements, and how human agency persists (or doesn't) within all this algorithmic mediation.
322.ww: This works as an analysis because it reveals that data-driven power is structural: analytical capacity becomes bargaining power. Those who can collect, model, and interpret data set the terms of the conversation before negotiators even sit down. The literature shows this pattern repeated across policy domains.
322.po: The review documents how big data and AI are reshaping policy negotiations by functioning as hidden sources of power. It matters because it signals that transparency, data literacy, and human oversight in policy contexts aren't optional—they're essential to keeping power balanced in democratic negotiations.

323.bp: This is a track description for the History of the Web conference. It asks: why does today's web look the way it does? What decisions, accidents, and institutions shaped it? And what do those historical lessons tell us about choices we're making today with AI and LLMs? The aim is to use history as a lens for understanding what is genuinely novel, what is repetition, and what remains unsolved.
323.wh: When a new technology emerges (like large language models applied to the web), there's a temptation to treat it as brand new, with no precedent. But the web's evolution has recurring tensions—relevance versus reliability, openness versus governance, scale versus accountability—that show up across decades. Missing this history means repeating old mistakes and misunderstanding what's actually new.
323.ap: The track traces a connected arc from early web ranking and information retrieval, through user experience and engagement platforms, to semantic web and knowledge graphs, and finally to today's LLMs and agentic AI. It positions LLMs as both trained on the web (the web as data) and evaluated against the web (the web as benchmark) and deployed on the web (the web as space of impact). The panel explores how historical decisions about relevance, curation, and openness shape what LLM-based systems can and should do.
323.ww: This works because technologies don't operate in a vacuum—they're shaped by decisions made in earlier eras, and those decisions encoded certain trade-offs (e.g., Google chose ranking for relevance over ranking for reliability, which worked until it didn't). Seeing those trade-offs historically helps us ask sharper questions about trade-offs in LLMs and agentic AI today.
323.po: The payoff is perspective: by seeing that relevance, openness, scale, and accountability have always been in tension on the web, we can recognize that these tensions aren't new problems for LLMs to solve, but recurring choices we need to make deliberately, informed by what worked and failed before.

324.bp: Quantum computers are incredible but error-prone—most of their output is noise. To use them reliably, you need to run error mitigation: techniques that cancel out noise mathematically. But if you're using a cloud-based quantum computer as a service, you have a problem: the service provider needs to see your circuit (the quantum program) to fix errors, but your circuit might be proprietary and valuable. How do you get error mitigation without revealing your secrets?
324.wh: The central tension: effective error mitigation requires understanding the circuit's structure and the noise model. A service provider can't do good mitigation if they only see aggregated statistics. But if you give them the full circuit and your noise assumptions, you've revealed your intellectual property. Standard solutions either leak information or don't mitigate well.
324.ap: Blind-QEM uses Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs): a cryptographic technique where one party proves a statement is true without revealing the statement itself. The customer commits to a circuit (via a cryptographic hash), then submits the quantum program to the provider. The provider performs noise mitigation using only aggregate statistics and logs of operations. At the end, ZKPs verify that the computation performed actually respected the committed circuit, without the provider ever seeing the circuit itself.
324.ww: This works because ZKPs let you prove 'I computed your program correctly' without revealing what the program is. The provider can infer some aggregate statistics about noise (how often certain errors occur) without seeing the circuit details. The commitment mechanism (like a cryptographic receipt) ensures the provider can't substitute a different circuit mid-computation.
324.po: Users can now outsource quantum error mitigation to cloud providers without revealing circuit topology or proprietary noise models. This matters because it makes cloud quantum computing viable for companies that don't want to reveal their algorithms.

325.bp: Imagine an academic conference where you're a program chair trying to assign papers to reviewers. Each paper requires effort to review (a paper on quantum computing takes longer than one on basic algorithms). Reviewers can bid on papers they want to review (zero effort) or get assigned papers they didn't bid on (takes real effort). How do you assign papers fairly—so no reviewer feels badly treated—while minimizing total reviewer burden?
325.wh: The obvious approach is to give everyone equally many papers. But that's not fair if some papers are much longer or harder. The challenge is a fairness notion called EFX (Envy-Free up to one item): no reviewer should feel so badly treated that they'd trade away even one of their papers to someone else. This is mathematically hard because of the asymmetry: a reviewer incurs zero cost if they bid on a paper, but full cost if they don't.
325.ap: The paper proposes an algorithm that computes an assignment satisfying both EFX fairness and MMS (Maximin Share: everyone gets at least their 'fair share' in the worst case). The algorithm constructs the assignment step by step, ensuring that the fairness guarantees hold throughout. It also achieves a 2-approximation of optimal social cost, meaning the total reviewer burden is at most twice the absolute minimum possible—optimal for this problem.
325.ww: This works because the algorithm carefully manages the two sources of cost: papers reviewers bid on (free) and papers they don't (costly). By ensuring that no reviewer can point to someone else's bundle and say 'I'd trade my papers for yours except one,' fairness is maintained. The cost approximation comes from a clever accounting of how reviewers and papers are matched.
325.po: Conference organizers can now assign papers both fairly and efficiently: reviewers feel their workload is reasonable, no one feels exploited, and the total effort is near-optimal. This matters because fairness in peer review directly impacts the scientific community's trust in results.

326.bp: Imagine a future where instead of you browsing Amazon or eBay, an AI agent does it for you—clicking through listings, reading reviews, comparing prices, and making a purchase decision. The question is: what will that agent actually buy, and why? Will its choices differ from yours? And if AI agents start making billions of e-commerce decisions, how does that reshape markets?
326.wh: We don't know how AI agents behave in e-commerce because they haven't been the dominant buyers yet. Different AI models (Claude, GPT-4, etc.) might rank products differently. A human might read one product as 'top of the list, must be good' but an AI might read 'top of the list, probably a paid ad, skip it.' We don't have systematic data on whether AI agents are fooled by fake reviews, position effects, or pricing tricks in the same ways humans are.
326.ap: The researchers built ACES, a sandbox: a simulated online marketplace that an AI agent can interact with, fully controllable. They paired an agent (GPT-4, Claude, others) with the mock marketplace and ran experiments. First, they looked at what each model bought from a fixed set of products. Then they randomized product positions, prices, review counts, and sponsored tags, and measured how much each factor changed each model's choice.
326.ww: This works because the sandbox lets you isolate which features drive choice. In the real world, when a product's price changes, its position also changes, its reviews change, everything is entangled. In the sandbox, you can move a product from row 3 to row 1 and see the exact effect. By testing multiple models, you see which biases are model-specific (learned during training) versus universal.
326.po: The study found that all models favor the top row, but different models prefer different columns, revealing model-specific biases. Models penalize sponsored tags and reward endorsements, and sensitivities to price, ratings, and reviews vary sharply. This matters because if AI agents become major e-commerce actors, their biases could reshape competition—some sellers could exploit those biases, while others get unfairly disadvantaged.

327.bp: Imagine a large machine learning model trained on graph data (like user-item networks for recommendations). You want to adapt it to a new domain (like a different set of items) without forgetting what it learned before. But you need to do this for many domains in sequence—one after another—without the model collapsing into chaos. How do you continuously adapt a graph model across many new domains without catastrophic forgetting?
327.wh: Standard fine-tuning causes catastrophic forgetting: after adapting to domain 2, the model forgets domain 1. Adding a regularizer (a penalty for changing too much) helps but hurts performance. Cross-domain adaptation is harder because domains have different graph structures. When you add adapters (small specialized models) for each domain, they can interfere with each other. And measuring what the model has learned across domains is hard because graph models don't learn explicit, comparable representations.
327.ap: G-CORMoL uses something called orthogonal mixture-of-experts with LoRA adapters. Each domain gets its own small adapter (LoRA), but these adapters are mathematically orthogonal—perpendicular in a high-dimensional space, so one adapter's changes don't interfere with another's. A routing network learns to blend the adapters dynamically, pulling in expertise from multiple past domains when needed. A contrastive objective (a training trick borrowed from self-supervised learning) pushes different adapters to specialize on different aspects of the problem.
327.ww: This works because orthogonality is a mathematical way to prevent interference: if you try to rotate vector A orthogonally and then apply changes to vector B (also orthogonal), changing B doesn't affect A. A router that learns a global policy means the model can reuse past adapters intelligently, enabling positive transfer. Contrastive specialization ensures each adapter learns something distinct.
327.po: The model can now adapt across many domains in sequence without forgetting prior domains and without degrading performance. It even gets better over time as it accumulates knowledge from past domains. This matters for recommendation systems and other applications where you want one model to serve multiple distinct user groups or item categories simultaneously.

328.bp: In social networks and graphs, communities are clusters of tightly-connected people. A common task is to identify the community a given user belongs to, starting only from knowing the user. If you know Alice, can you find her community without exploring the entire network? This is called local community detection and is useful for real-time recommendation and personalization.
328.wh: The standard approach starts with a seed node (Alice) and expands outward, adding neighboring nodes until you've traced out the full community. But this expansion is prone to accumulated errors: each step depends on the previous step, so mistakes compound. If the seed node is on the boundary (at the edge of a community rather than the core), the expansion can easily drift into a neighboring community. Semi-supervised methods use a few labeled examples to help, but weak supervision makes it hard to correct accumulated errors.
328.ap: SLFM (Semi-Supervised Local community detection based on hyperbolic Flow Matching) reframes the problem as generative: instead of expanding outward, think of it as transporting probability distributions. Start with a distribution centered on the seed node, then use a learned vector field to transform that distribution into one centered on the full community. The system has three pieces: a Seed Selector that uses hyperbolic geometry to validate and improve the seed node, a Flow Transporter that learns how to smoothly morph distributions, and a Community Expander that uses the transported distribution as guidance.
328.ww: This works because treating community detection as transport of probability distributions lets you smooth out accumulated errors—you're not making discrete expansion decisions but learning a continuous path. Hyperbolic geometry is good at modeling hierarchical structures (central, core nodes are near the origin; peripheral nodes are far out), so the seed selector can validate whether your starting point is central or boundary. The flow transporter is learned from weak labels and naturally handles partial information.
328.po: The system is robust to bad seed nodes and weak supervision, finding communities even when you start from a boundary user. This matters for real-time recommendation systems that need to quickly identify user communities for personalization without expensive expansion.

329.bp: Online platforms host billions of pieces of content—memes, images with text, videos, news articles—that can spread misinformation, hate speech, or propaganda. Moderating this at scale is impossible by hand, so platforms use AI. But today's moderation tools work with text or images separately. What if you could use multiple types of signals together—text, images, even temporal patterns across platforms—to understand and moderate multimodal content better?
329.wh: A meme is a single image with text overlaid; hatespeech requires understanding both together. A video showing something suspicious might only become obviously problematic when combined with the audio narration. And a narrative that's okay in isolation becomes dangerous when amplified by coordinated sharing across platforms. Most AI systems are built for single modalities (text only, image only) and miss these cross-modal nuances.
329.ap: MM4SG 2026 (the fourth workshop on Multimedia Content Analysis for Social Good) convened researchers from NLP, computer vision, machine learning, computational social science, and ethics to tackle multimodal moderation. A major theme was how to use large vision-language models (VLMs)—models that reason about both images and text together—and agentic systems (AI systems that act autonomously) to scale moderation. The workshop emphasized interpretability and ethical grounding, not just accuracy.
329.ww: This works because treating content as inherently multimodal captures the full story. A hateful image gains its power from the text overlay; a false claim gains traction from the authority signaled by a video. By reasoning over multiple modalities, systems can catch context that single-modality tools miss. Agentic systems can make decisions autonomously but with human oversight.
329.po: The workshop aimed to advance the state of the art in detecting and moderating synthetic content, memes, and cross-platform narratives. This matters because platforms serve billions of people, and moderation at that scale requires AI that understands context, not just pattern matching—and because decisions about speech have real social impact.
